result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, apologies that curdled into silence, jokes that died on the vine. There's one to my mother from three years ago. "Mom, I know you're worried about—" and then nothing. I don't remember what I was going to say. Probably something about my job, or my apartment, or the way I've started drinking wine alone on Tuesdays and calling it self-care.

The folder has 47 items. I counted once, then stopped counting. Some are to people I haven't spoken to in years. Some are to people I see every day. The proximity doesn't matter. What matters is the gap between what I feel and what I say, and how that gap widens with each passing hour until the words feel foreign, like speaking a language I once knew but have forgotten.

My therapist says I have trouble with vulnerability. She says it like it's a diagnosis, which I suppose it is. "You intellectualize your emotions," she told me last month. "You turn them into essays instead of letting them be messy." I nodded. I always nod. Then I went home and wrote a 2,000-word analysis of why I nod in therapy sessions.

There's something about the written word that feels safer. It can be edited. It can be deleted. It can sit in a folder, unseen, until the phone dies and takes it with it. Speaking is different. Speaking is immediate. Speaking is a commitment. You can't unsay the thing you blurted out at 2 AM when the wine has loosened your tongue and your defenses.

I think about my father sometimes. He died when I was twenty-three, which is young enough to still feel like a child and old enough to know better. We didn't speak for the last two years of his life. There was a fight. There are always fights. I don't remember what it was about anymore, only the shape of it—his voice rising, mine shutting down, the door closing with a sound like finality. I wrote him a letter after he died. I never sent it. It's in the folder. I read it sometimes, and I can't tell if it's forgiveness or just more performance, another essay dressed up as grief.

The thing about unsent messages is that they become their own kind of relationship. You maintain a version of someone in your head, a dialogue that only exists in one direction. My mother, in my drafts, is always understanding, always patient. The real her is more complicated. She calls too often and not often enough. She asks about my love life with a hopefulness that makes me want to hide. She sends me articles about depression and anxiety, as if I haven't spent my adult life managing both. I love her. I don't know how to tell her that without it sounding like a complaint.

I met someone last winter. Her name was Clara, and she had a laugh that sounded like breaking glass—sharp and surprising and a little dangerous. We talked for six hours in a bar that was closing around us, and I felt something unlock in my chest, some door I'd forgotten was there. Then I went home and wrote her a message that was too long, too earnest, too *much*. I deleted it. I wrote another. Deleted that too. By morning, I'd convinced myself that I'd imagined the connection, that it was just the whiskey and the loneliness and the particular sadness of a Tuesday in January.

She texted me three days later. "Had fun last night. We should do it again." I stared at the message for an hour. Then I wrote: "Yeah. Definitely." Three words. Safe. Forgettable. She didn't reply. I told myself that was fine. I told myself a lot of things.

The folder grows. It's almost full now, 47 drafts taking up space I'll never reclaim. Sometimes I wonder what would happen if I sent them all at once, a burst of honesty that would probably destroy every relationship I have. Or maybe it would save them. Maybe the weight of all that unsaid is what's actually killing us, slowly, one unspoken truth at a time.

I don't know. I'm still writing. That's the thing about words—they keep coming, even when no one's listening. Especially then.
